utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It's P3855.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see a document on my screen now. Yes. Apparently if it's paragraph 7, it's in its entirety in B/C/S on the screen. However, for the English we should move to the next page after two lines. Could you please restart reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Certainly. And, Your Honour, you were quite right with respect to Witness Wilson's statement, it was paragraphs 41 through 43 which address the 14th of May shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: "The use of the Ministry units in co-ordinated action with the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of BH may be ordered by the minister of interior, commander of the police detachment --"

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page. Yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: "... of the ministry for the Sarajevo CSB and the chief of the CSB of the ministry (for the territory under his jurisdiction). "Commander of the police detachment and chiefs of CSB shall inform the Ministry Staff of any use of the units described in the preceding paragraph. "While participating in combat operations, the units of the ministry shall be subordinated to the command of the armed forces; however, the ministry units shall be under the direct command of certain Ministry officials." And that's the end of paragraph 7, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Well, we don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the English --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- there's no number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, number 8 now appears.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that, in fact, in participating --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I've lost my original question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That rather than having the co-operative relationship with the Serbian MUP, and I'll add it's described in paragraph 36 of your statement, that when it came to combat, the Serbian MUP in fact was subordinated to your command.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the question? The Serbian MUP was not subordinated to the command in any respect, the command of the 4th Corps that is. Nor did the 4th Corps command command MUP. I do not exclude a possibility of a unit like a platoon or a company joining the territorial component of the Serbian republic in co-ordination in case of the JNA being attacked by the other side as it happened on a number of occasions in that period. It was the period of truce where the units should have -- leave Sarajevo from their barracks to go to the FRY. We can see in this order by Minister Stanisic that he ordered that the Ministry of the Interior shall be in command. Not even their territorial component.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd note it is break time. I have less than ten minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Defence, whether you'd prefer to have the break to prepare for re-examination or whether you would prefer to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We could take the break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break now. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back in -- at 10 minutes past 12.00. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just verify whether the videolink is still functioning well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I confirm that we can see you and we can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Bibles, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, over the break I've determined there is no further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one matter I would like to raise. Ms. Bibles, you have put to the witness a few questions about telephone conversations about what happened on the 14th of May, discussions about targets. The witness explained that he didn't follow-up the orders, et cetera. Now, does that contradict the Prosecution's case in that respect? Because then it would be fair to put it to the witness. And it's even required by the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: There won't be any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- do that exercise so that the witness has an opportunity to comment on what, in the Prosecution's view, happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard the Judge's discussion and you've heard me put several questions to you about targeting different locations that you were asked to -- to target by at least two different individuals in intercepts we've heard, and you've heard me explain that the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that on the 14th of May there was shelling in Sarajevo. You have denied all of that. And so I would put it to you that your testimony has not been accurate in that regard. What would you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of May Sarajevo was not shelled. This is a completely different concept. There was fire at the periphery of the elevation point between Rajlovac and Sarajevo in order to prevent the attack of Muslim forces on the Rajlovac neighbourhood, because the day before the Muslim forces carried out a massacre of the Serb population in the area of Sarajevo called Pofalici. So in order to prevent something like that from happening again, the JNA fired and was obliged to prevent any massacres on any of the population, and that is different from the concept of shelling. Please, there was no shelling. I have been living in Sarajevo -- Novo Sarajevo for 27 years, so I have been the recipient of awards from the city of Sarajevo. I am a citizen of Sarajevo. So my task was, as the corps commander, to bring out members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army without any casualties or losses. These were people who had been blocked in the barracks inside Sarajevo, and I was supposed to protect those who were threatened, regardless of whether they were Serbs or Muslims, as much as I was able to. This was not my war. This was the war of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I said that to the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. Personally to the President Alija Izetbegovic on the 2nd of May. And I proposed that they resolve that in a different way, but that was up to them. That was not up to me. JNA units were engaged only in areas where they were defending themselves. If they were defending a barracks, they were defending a barracks. If they were defending their positions outside of the barracks, they would be defended. It did not attack anyone anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of defending, and I believe you -- in your answer, you indicated that the JNA fired, isn't it true that the JNA used heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's called heavy artillery. Multi-calibre artillery. It's 120-millimetres. It does not even belong in the category of artillery. It's treated as infantry weaponry, which is more precise at shorter ranges. Multi-calibre artillery of the corps was located behind, in a village behind Pale called Sokolac, and that artillery did not fire and was not used. Only the artillery that was located in the Lukavica area was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps one follow-up question for the witness. The Prosecution has presented evidence which includes that firing on or around the 14th of May was estimated to include 5- to 10.000 rounds of artillery of having been fired onto the city on that day. Do you have any comment on that evidence about the numbers of rounds fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [via videolink] That's just as I said. It's a distorted picture about the number of artillery weapons. So we have another distorted picture about the number of projectiles fired. Usually one burst of fire is fired from ten weapons, and that would be ten projectiles in an area of 500 metres in front of the attacking forces in order to warn them not to proceed, otherwise they would suffer casualties. And that is the role of the JNA artillery. That is what they did, and this was not done in the city of Sarajevo. This would be something completely different. The fire was executed in an unpopulated area, where the actual town garbage dump is located. General MacKenzie can testify to this. I was in touch with him and agreed with him on certain things as well as Fikret Abdic who was the representative of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have one other question for you. You were asked to comment on firing at elevation 695. You said: "Artillery fire was of the barrage type, and the firing was executed in agreement with the other side between the attackers and the defenders in order to prevent the attackers from breaking through and to get them to return to their positions." Could you tell us where the -- one second, please -- where the intercept, as far as I could hear, does not refer to any agreement. Could you tell us whether that agreement is recorded somewhere or could you tell us how that agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [via videolink] The agreement was reached between representatives of the Serbian republic, the Muslim representatives, representatives of the JNA from the General Staff, which was there as a negotiating team with the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was in the presence of the UNPROFOR commander. There was no representative of the European community. He had already left Sarajevo. This was in the building of UNPROFOR where their seat and command was. A non-attack agreement was signed and then in the case of attack there would be fire directed at the side that was attacking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the -- one second, please. So the agreement was that if one of the parties would attack, that the other party would respond to such an attack. Is that how I have to understand the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [via videolink] Precisely. Of course. The side that is attacked has to defend themselves. That is inevitable. The massacre in Pofalici that occurred the day before played a part in this defensive action, and this is something that General MacKenzie was well aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I remember well, in that telephone conversation, you were asked to fire at a certain position without any further explanation why you would have to fire at that position. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [via videolink] Yes, you understood me correctly. It was precisely in order to prevent the attacker from coming to the Rajlovac settlement and again committing a massacre against the Serbian population, which had occurred the day before in Pofalici. I think that was also a factor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that none of that appears in the telephone conversation where just a request to fire at a certain position is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [via videolink] Well, you know, I agree with you. There was just the request in the telephone conversation for this to be done and thereby this problem is resolved of having the attacker reach the Rajlovac neighbourhood. That settled that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Colonel, you will be re-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is, as I told you before, is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I have just a few questions for you. First of all, during May 1992, what were the standing orders from your JNA superiors relating to the use of heavy weapons against civilian targets; that is to say, were civilians allowed to be targeted and if so under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it was prohibited in the strictest of terms to use artillery, not only on civilian targets but on targets whereby the civilian population would be jeopardised, because the other side used areas in neighbourhoods to fire at barracks, at JNA units, and Territorial Defence units of Republika Srpska. And if there was a response to that fire, then it would be said that the Serb side was firing at the civilian population. Use of higher artillery weaponry from April until late May was exclusively under the authority of the commander of the military district. A lower-ranking commander did not have the right to use such heavy weaponry unless previously approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to turn to a document the Prosecution used, Exhibit P02728. And as we wait for that document, I can say that this is the conversation recorded between Milos Baros, yourself, and General Mladic that you said was in relation to the cadets that were blockaded in the barracks. If we -- first of all, could you describe for us --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us what were the conditions that the cadets were facing in the barracks at that time being the 11th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's necessary to have the B/C/S and not the English twice on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. We should have the same number. It should be -- yeah, 2728. It should have a B/C/S component.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We had the B/C/S previously during cross-examination on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, sir, again my question is: Could you describe for us, what were the conditions that the cadets were facing in the barracks at that time; being, the 11th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The cadets in the Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo were blockaded on the 2nd and the 3rd of May. From that day on, they were exposed to sporadic fire from mortars and they were shelled when they were in the barracks compound. Two civilian employees were killed who worked in the canteen of the Marsal Tito military school. The units that were firing every day were forcing those cadets, those kids who were blockaded there, to hold on to their weapons and to try to save their lives. So you can imagine what psychological state they were in when they were exposed to that. Because of that, we tried to make sure that they weren't hungry or thirsty. Everything else meant that they were sealed off and exposed to shooting every day. Their position was a difficult one, both in physical and psychological terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, this document, this conversation that is recorded, at page 3 in both versions identifies that there are approximately 280 cadets that are stuck in the facility. Were there any estimations as to the number of opposing forces that were blockading these 280 cadets?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The -- well, you could leave the barracks only from four gates. The gates were guarded by four battalions of the Muslim side, which would make sure the exits were covered by fire. Any attempt to exit meant that the cadets were exposed to danger. That's why they were waiting for a peaceful resolution. Unfortunately, that barracks was the last one to be deblocked in Sarajevo. On the 5th of June, I had already left Sarajevo by that time. That was the 5th of June, 1992. The youth there was not trained for armed combat. They were trained to lead the units. So even though that was so, they were in such a situation that they were forced to fight for their -- fight to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, for those that are less militarily trained, the four battalions of the Muslim forces, what would the numeric strength be of those combined four battalions?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The four battalions that were blocking were not completely in keeping with the establishment. Some of them numbered 200 or 400 or 600 men. But in any case, we did not want it to permit any of the cadets to get killed when they were leaving the barracks. Their lives were the most precious thing that we had, so we wanted to do everything to prevent them from getting killed. That was one thing. The other thing: If the unit had tried to break out of the barracks, it would have encountered the next in line Muslim units that were located in Sarajevo. According to their statements, these units numbered between 50- and 70.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in some answers to some prior questions you've identified Fikret Abdic as the BH representative for negotiations. To your knowledge, did General Mladic have any specific conversations with Fikret Abdic to try and resolve the issue of the barricaded cadets?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic had several talks with Fikret Abdic when he took over as the commander of the 2nd Military District. One of the talks he conducted by telephone from my office. I was present for that because before that I had spoken to Abdic. General Mladic arrived and then he joined that conversation with Abdic. And it was about the following: He first asked Fikret Abdic, calling him Babo, I don't know if they knew each other from before or not. He said, "Come on, let's settle our problems between ourselves. The two of us speak the same language. You are from Kladusa, I am from Kali Novik. So let's not allow others who arrive and who speak differently to be the ones to resolve our problems." Fikret Abdic replied, "Perhaps it's too late for that, General." And then Mladic said, "It's never too late if the two of us try and if we have the will to resolve this peacefully." Then he asked him to go and visit his mother's house, which the Muslim forces had torched a few days before, and to check whether his mother had burned down in the house. His brother had a house in Pofalici and that's where his mother lived and that house was set on fire. Mr. Abdic said that I was informed that the artillery units had set it on fire when they were shelling. And then Mladic said, "Right. They set my house on fire and my house happens to be between two Muslim houses, those are my neighbours, and neither of those houses had burned down. So look at that, Babo. You can see what kind of artillery I have."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to call up document P3855.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise again. This is the document that you do not have with you in Belgrade. It is the document issued by Mr. Stanisic to the MUP forces. And I would like to ask you about the terminology used. We saw in paragraph 7 of the same that they were talking about co-ordinated action. Could you please explain for us what is co-ordinated action as opposed to resubordination in JNA military jargon?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Co-ordinated action is if several units are engaged in the Defence of an area or a barracks, then they co-ordinate the fire amongst themselves that is directed at the attackers. According to regulations, you can only have one command, so then the fire is directed in co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, could you explain for us what is the difference between that scenario and the classic scenario of resubordination in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we are talking about resubordination, that means that that unit would be completely subordinated to the command or the specific commander conducting an operation or the defence of an area or a barracks. When you have co-ordination, then you have co-ordinated fire of units who are not necessarily under one single command. For example, there was a police station at Vrace from the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. At the same time, you had a Yugoslav Peoples' Army unit which was guarding the monuments from World War II of executed Serbs and Jews. And then you had a command post of the corps command. And now if an attack occurred on any one of those structures, then fire would be co-ordinated so that there would be co-ordinated firing at the enemy, and it does not necessarily mean that each one of these elements was subordinated to the one and the same command. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you asked about resubordination. The witness explained that resubordination would mean that there would be complete subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the text of the document clearly talks about subordination, although apparently in a certain sense limited, that the command of the unit itself would still be in the hands of certain ministry officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the resubordination seems to be a different concept. At least that's how I understand the testimony, it being that the direct command of certain ministry officials would certainly then govern the internal functioning of that unit but the unit in itself being subordinated, at least I have -- I'm trying to fully understand the document. But to say this has got nothing to do with subordination is -- sounds a bit odd, where the document itself says: "The units of the ministry shall be subordinated to the command of the armed forces." The -- it looks as if the witness says that that's not what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would note that the document comes from a police official not from an army official such that their understanding of terminology may be different and that's why I ask for the military understanding of the term in my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whether that resolves the issue is a -- it seems then that at least the police officials considered themselves to be subordinated, if it comes from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, they also use the term "co-ordinated action" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- so I think that they distinguish between different scenarios.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd just have one other question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just -- I just did raise the issue so that you have an opportunity to further elaborate on it if you wish to do so and not to hide from you that the appearance of the word "subordination" seems not to be without relevance for me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness could wait for the next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the document signed by the Police Minister of Interior Mico Stanisic says: "While participating in combat operations the units of the ministry shall be subordinated to the command of the armed forces; however, the ministry units shall be under the direct command of certain ministry officials." The first question I'd like to ask you: Did you ever plan any combat operations at the JNA 4th Corps in May to June 1992 that included police forces from the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: One small digression to the question or actually to the minister's order. He did not state decisively in the order to whom the police was to be subordinated, but it was to be subordinated to the armed forces. I believe that this was done in the period when the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was being formed. This is the period from the 14th of May. There was still six days left before that setting up of the corps was to be completed by establishment. So in that sense, he maintained the right to command the police but at certain points it was being resubordinated to the armed forces. It does not say that it was being resubordinated to the command of the JNA 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. And the Prosecution insinuated that the police were under your command, so I'm asking you: Did you ever plan any combat operations at the JNA 4th Corps in May to June 1992 involving police forces?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Never. Not a single operation involved their participation. While I was there, they were not intended for combat operations. They were there only to regulate the situation in the territory of the Serbian republic; in this specific case, the municipalities of Ilidza and Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I thank you on behalf of myself and my client, General Ratko Mladic, for your answers to my questions. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, any further questions for the witness triggered by the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber has no questions either. Mr. Gagovic, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for making yourself available as a witness and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, this concludes the videolink testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Defence. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you prefer to start with the testimony of the witness and then to interrupt it after some 20 minutes, take a break, and then -- or would you prefer to start after a break? We then take a break until ten minutes past 1.00, and would have another 65 minutes to go. I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would take the other offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would take the second option. Then that's how we'll proceed. We'll take a break and we will resume at 10 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, I'll just deal with one matter related to Witness Indjic. Last week Witness Indjic testified before this Chamber. During the course of his testimony, the witness made references to notes which he keeps at his house. The witness agreed to make these notes available to the Tribunal but requested that an officer of the Tribunal accompany him. On the 4th of September, the Chamber requested the Registrar to appoint an officer responsible for the chain of custody of the notes after being handed over. The confidential status of this decision is hereby lifted. During the witness's testimony, the Chamber also ordered the witness as well as anyone else not to destroy or dispose of the notes. The Registry informed the Chamber in the afternoon of the 4th of September of this year that the witness had expressed some hesitation about handing over the notes voluntarily. It was then clarified to the witness that there was no order from the Chamber about having to hand them over and that it was entirely up to him whether he would hand over the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have received news from the Registry that the witness has handed over the notes and that they are currently in the possession of the Registry. And this concludes this statement. Good afternoon, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, unless you have any problem in standing, could I invite you to stand. But if you would prefer to remain seated, please do so. The Rules require you to make a solemn declaration. The next is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration. Mr. Usher, have you handed out the -- well, if you have difficulties in standing, then -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Please be seated. Mr. Lukic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, you'll find him to your left, is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Lukic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, please tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Vladimir Lukic. I was born in 1933 in Sanski Most in the village of Dabar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 65 ter 1D02457 on the screens. It is Mr. Lukic's statement. I would kindly ask the usher to hand over a hard copy of the statement to Mr. Lukic. The Prosecution has already been convinced that it is a clean copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you recall having provided a statement to members of Mr. Karadzic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please turn over to the last page.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement bearing my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The statement originates from the Karadzic case, thus we may have some issues with the numbers. However, I hope that Mr. Traldi and I will be able to point you to the right paragraph of the statement so as to avoid any confusion. Is the statement you provided accurate and truthful as given to Mr. Karadzic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: It is absolutely truthful and it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you basically provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt that I would respond to those questions the way I already have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, we would like to tender Professor Lukic's statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1D2457 will be D626.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read out the shortened version of Mr. Lukic's statement and will have only a few questions following that. [In English] May I do so, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In early June 1992, Vladimir Lukic was appointed commissioner for the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. From July the 1st until 19th of December, 1992, Vladimir Lukic worked as a representative of the Republika Srpska at the UNPROFOR in Sarajevo. Vladimir Lukic received many reports about crimes against Serbs in Sarajevo. He passed on all reports and eye-witness accounts to the UNPROFOR but did not receive satisfactory responses. Vladimir Lukic found UNPROFOR to be negatively disposed towards the Serbian side in a number of respects. UNPROFOR was inconsistent in enforcing the ban on firing from its immediate vicinity. It was further always assumed without checking that shelling was committed by Serbs. He observed that when Serbian artillery fired at a target in the city, it was always a military target, although UNPROFOR would nonetheless describe it as a civilian target. UNPROFOR, according to Professor Lukic, was aware of the Muslim snipers in Sarajevo. In mid-December 1992, Vladimir Lukic was offered by Radovan Karadzic to be prime minister of the new government and he accepted that offer. The position of the government was that all citizens of the RS, regardless of ethnicity, must be guaranteed freedom of movement according to their freely expressed will. The government constantly called for the establishment of the rule of law and the protection of all citizens including refugees regardless of ethnicity. This included ordering the ministries of interior and defence and the security service of the VRS to use all legal means to protect civilians and their property regardless of ethnicity. The electricity situation in Republika Srpska was dramatically bad which affected all sides of society. The Muslim side repeatedly cut power supply lines. The government of Republika Srpska called for the unhindered passage of humanitarian convoys to both Muslims and Croats. The government tried, with all its powers, to prevent private and illegal relocation of refugees and demanded that criminal proceedings be initiated against those who were involved in such activities. The government experienced significant problems with the municipalities which functioned as states within a state with significant power. The presidency and the government fought to centralise government in keeping with the constitution. This was statement summary of Professor Lukic and with your leave I would just pose several questions for this -- for our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we please have document 1D02443 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, it has to do with paragraph 20 of your statement. I wanted to remind you of the numbers. The number we will be referring to is different from the number used in the previous case. A corresponding table was provided to the Prosecution and the Chamber for their perusal. As you can see on the screen, it was a -- the Elektroprivreda company of Republika Srpska that issued the document. It's subcompany Distribucija Pale. On the 11th of January, 1993, it informed the government of Republika Srpska - it says to prime minister Vladimir Lukic personally - of some apply and distribution issues in Visegrad, Rogatica, Sokolac, Pale and Vogosca. Do you recall having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Certainly I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last sentence. You said: "Certainly I do." And what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear your last sentence when I asked if you recalled the document.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I do recall the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you come a bit closer to the microphone, Mr. Lukic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you recall about this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: The moment I arrived in Pale I saw there was no electricity and that the generators were used to power it. It became clear to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Stop for a moment, Professor. It is in the statement already. But do you recall anything specific as regards this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I remember that we took measures to have electricity brought from Visegrad to Rogatica and Pale as well as Sokolac, and to have electricity supplied to Vogosca where the military production facilities were. We managed to do so by going to Rogatica and conducting a meeting there with our unit commander. We asked of him to move the front line held by Muslims, because they regularly fired at our power cables cutting off electricity in the process. He promised to do so to vice-president to Mr. Koljevic, to Mr. Tolimir and myself, to do so. He indeed did manage to push back enemy positions by some 4 to 4 and a half kilometres. With the help of our electrical company as well as a number of people from Serbia who also required electricity, because we provided electricity to them from our hydroelectric plant, we managed to bring electricity to all of the settlements I enumerated. More importantly, our military equipment production was set in motion in Vogosca. There was no further need in those locations for the power generators, meaning we no longer had to use fuel for lightening and other needs. I think it was a very important step which we did at the outset. Later on, we managed to bring electricity to some other of our settlements around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our case it is 1D02445.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It has to do with paragraph 74 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you deal with the document during the testimony of the witness, you could tender that and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and reduce the number of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because I agree with the Prosecution that I will -- if you have their e-mail, there was objection by the Prosecution regarding six documents from our list. I will tender only two from bunch of these six, and I will not tender other four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I then still do not know which ones --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's deal with as many --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- documents as possible during the testimony of the witness and what then remains, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would then tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D2443 will be Exhibit D627.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D627 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the next one I would like to have in the e-court is 1D02445.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the document before us, Professor. It is a decision on the appointment of a republican commissioner in the municipality of Odzak. In the signature block we see the name Vladimir Lukic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is you, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that the date is the 19th of February, 1994. How come commissioners were still being appointed to municipalities at the time if you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to recall each and every event, but it is worth mentioning the fact that Republika Srpska at the time functioned as a confederation of municipalities. Depending on their individual financial status, they tried to be as independent as possible. What was important was that in this particular municipality, there was a tendency -- well, I think they wanted to command the armed forces themselves as well as to govern some other aspects of life and society. We revoked that right and the commissioner was appointed to bring it within some normal limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see the decision itself but did the commissioner indeed take over his duty and work in the field?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. For a short period of time before the municipalities were finally organised. We later attempted to have each and every municipality properly set up with its municipal assembly, the council, and so on and so forth. At that time, all of the commissioners, of whom there were many by that time, gradually left their positions leaving the job to municipality organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. This was all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if, Your Honour, you want me to explain on each paragraphs those documents I'm not going to tender refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But perhaps first --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This one I would tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This one you would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D2445 will Exhibit D628, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, there is a large number of associated exhibits, isn't it? Some of them have, I think it -- we started at 89, which is certainly above the number that the Chamber would be inclined to accept unless there was any precise explanation as to why we need them. That's one issue. The second issue is that although many of the documents are anything between one and five pages, there are still some 15 between the 10 and the 20 pages, but we have certainly also documents which go well beyond 20 pages going up to 285 pages or 466 pages, the very long ones. Do we really need all that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. What we need is the portion of the document discussed by the witness in his statement. Very often, even if it's a 60-page document, it's referred only to one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- uploaded, is only the one paragraph uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we don't have the -- because we used the Karadzic statement and documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- yes. But we have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to try to organise that in a different way because if there are 466 pages in evidence of one of these documents, then the Chamber will read it and will rely on 466 pages. That's how we work. So therefore it's up to you, perhaps, to agree with Mr. Traldi what are the relevant pages and to ask Mr. Traldi whether he would like to add pages for purposes of context and then to come to a conclusion what need to be tendered. And then, of course, we would need certainly a table of concordance --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that in the list we saw that the new numbers are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if we have reduced sized documents, then of course we need a new table of concordance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will -- now you have chart of concordance 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- but that's the 65 ter numbers as -- as they are used now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it -- unless you want to reduce under the same 65 ter number the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll agree with the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- which is the best way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then this still does is not resolve the huge number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you thought about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is our only witness that comes from the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we thought that it's necessary for us to include as many documents as possible through the witness, and he has the personal knowledge of I think almost every single document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we proposed to be admitted with his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there are also four documents without an English translation if I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I am well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I spoke with Mr. Traldi this morning and I asked him if he wants me to read paragraphs that we want -- actually, that were discussed in the statement of Professor Lukic, and Mr. Traldi told me that it's not necessary. But if Your Honours think that I should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I had meant that I thought it would be more efficient to request a translation of those paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- not that they should be admitted without a version in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We asked for translation of those whole documents, but those documents could be MFI'd then before the translation is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest, Mr. Lukic, that we'll start with the cross-examination now, that you'll prepare a new list of what still remains, what your plans are, with -- whether or not to translate, whether there is any agreement with Mr. Traldi in reducing the size of it, and that you present that tomorrow. So that's -- and then we'll discuss whether -- what can be admitted and what should be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only I'm afraid that maybe by tomorrow, we will not be able to have those short versions of the documents in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you have an agreement with Mr. Traldi, that's a good start. And then the -- perhaps on your list, you put it short version still to be uploaded into e-court so that we know that there is an agreement, that we know how many pages there are, but that we also know that we cannot yet MFI it but that we'll then reserve a number for it so that we proceed in the most efficient way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, on a related note and for completeness, I note that there are a couple of documents, 65 ter 1D02506, I believe, is one example, for which a partial translation has already been uploaded and the B/C/S is complete. My understanding after speaking to my learned friend is that the Defence is relying only on the portions of those documents which have been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's limited to that. Okay. We'll look at your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But in these cases, the relevant part of -- in B/C/S should be uploaded as a new document so that it corresponds perfectly with the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we'd just ask, perhaps, for the precision of the record, many of these are minutes, that the cover page be uploaded too so that it's identifiable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps, needless to say, that a few of the documents that were on the your associated exhibit list are already in evidence. I think that we have identified three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think it may be four now. I think one was admitted last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be four now. Yes, that could be. So if you please keep that in mind as well and now come with a now consolidated list in which all this information is put together and that we -- so that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having dealt with that, Mr. Lukic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You'll find Mr. Traldi to your right. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I'm sorry, were you able to receive interpretation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Could I please have the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there seems to be a problem. Could the usher assist. Let's see whether you're on the right channel and whether all the -- can you still not hear my -- Mr. -- can you hear the interpretation of what I say now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can hear it now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you mention in paragraph 5 of your statement that you knew Professor Koljevic before the war and you say: "We had identical views on the prewar situation in the former Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially Sarajevo." And you're referring here to Professor Nikola Koljevic, a member of the Republika Srpska presidency during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you also mention there that on one occasion in, 1991, you met with Radovan Karadzic. He was then the president of the SDS; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 31216 be brought to our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And while it comes up, you and Mr. Karadzic discussed the best way to link the Krajina with the Semberija region; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: We did not discuss anything. He just put one question to me and that was what was the best link between Krajina and Bijeljina; i.e., the eastern part of Republika Srpska. And I answered that it's always the route along the valley, that would be the right bank of the Sava River, where the road goes today and it always went in that direction towards Brcko and Bijeljina. And that was all of our conversation on that topic. The two of us did not have any other conversations at that time. We didn't even know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, if you look at your screen, this is a map you marked in the Karadzic trial, it shows the length that you recommended; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. That's that route. You cannot mark that road precisely on this map because there are some distortions, but you could understand that as the approximate route. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you recommended this route because it was the easy to defend; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I recommended the route because all the roads leading to Bijeljina were more or less closed. They were closed from May 1990 onwards, and then in mid-1990 all the roads were closed or dangerous. So that was that route. It would be easier if we wanted a firm position. It's always to defend a mountain or a hill road rather than a road in a valley from the point of view of defence. But when we are talking about traffic, then we know that valley roads are better than mountain roads and that they are the most favourable routes for laying down roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd tender this document, 65 ter 31216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6726, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just in relation to your last documents about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask that we have 65 ter 31218, page 36 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This will be the transcript of the first day of your testimony in the Karadzic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we'll be starting at line 25. So we'll continue to the top of the next page in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were asked to mark this map, and you said: "Now, Dr. Lukic, the usher will assist you with the pen, and I'd like on you to please draw that link," turning to next page, "between Krajina and Semberija through the Sava River valley that you proposed to Dr. Karadzic in 1991." And you answered, "This isn't" -- and as you said today: "This isn't very precise, I apologise. But along the right bank of the Sava, of course wherever you could go through. And this is the right way in all weather conditions, and the easy to defend." So you testified in the Karadzic trial that you were recommending the easiest route to defend, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I did probably say that, but the most important feature of a valley route would be for traffic, for roads, and it's much easier than mountain roads. But if you want to be very precise, then a hill road is always more easily defended, especially the one that goes to the highest parts, to the crests of the feature. But they are not so easy if we have inclement weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you've -- sir, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. I just wanted to say something more. That people who are not well versed in that don't know. When we say "defence," it can be defence from floods, from avalanches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- from different other serious threats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Mr. Traldi asked you whether you were recommending the easiest route, and then you started explaining a lot. Mr. Traldi then tried to interrupt you, and you showed irritation and you wanted to continue. You went well beyond the question. Mr. Traldi can interrupt you in order to take you back to what he asked you. There is no reason at that point in time where you went beyond what Mr. Traldi asked you to show any irritation or to continue as you wish rather than to follow the questions that are put to you by Mr. Traldi. Let that be clear. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, actually, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And we're still in your Karadzic testimony. You discussed communications problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in beginning on line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You'd discussed communications problems in the Republika Srpska. And directing your attention to lines 16 at the end of the line through 20. You said: "And I believe that it is clear to you that since the Croatian side and the Muslim side had established their forces much earlier, we were already -- we already had fears that this communication problem would cost us many lives." So while I appreciate the topographical insight you've provided today, I'd put to you that in the Karadzic case, you were in fact discussing defence in the typical sense: Defence against Croatian and Muslim forces, defence against the possibility that they would cost you many lives. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you cannot just neglect that because we were cut off in that entire area and later as well. No one from the Banja Luka or Krajina area, both Krajinas, could cross to Bijeljina. And perhaps it's not so nice and it's a notorious fact that because there were shortages of medicines, patients in Banja Luka were dieing because they could not get the medicines they needed, particularly well known among these events was the death of 12 babies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That event that you referred to just now, that was in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Early 1992, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But after you'd had this discussion -- sorry, after you'd made this recommendation to President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Correct. But the roads were already practically cut. Many in Bosnia and Herzegovina, particularly those to Croatia for Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was as early as 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That will complete my questions about this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 03202 be brought to the screen. This will be the transcript of a meeting between President Tudjman, Professor Koljevic, and Mr. Franjo Boras in Zagreb [Realtime transcript read in error "Zvornik Brigade"] in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you about a couple of Professor Koljevic's comments keeping in mind your statement that you and he agreed on all matters about prewar Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could begin by looking at page 8 in the English and 10 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I think you said that this conversation took place in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I did, and I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour. I see that perhaps my speed was off. I apologise, and I'll try to be more careful. I'd asked for 03202. Several years earlier and in a different country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Traldi, I observe that you added that the witness agreed on all matters. That's not what the statement says. We had identical views on the prewar situation. That is not necessarily "all." You added that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes I agree in main areas with someone without necessarily agreeing on every single item.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to explore some of the details of that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine, but I just wanted to insist on accuracy in quoting the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. While you had this conversation with Mr. Traldi, there was no translation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh. Is there -- is there translation now, Mr. Lukic? Yes. While --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you were able to follow, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was able to follow, but maybe this wording by Mr. Traldi would be good to have repeated but "all."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think it is for the witness irrelevant but for Mr. Mladic it may be. But I don't know whether he received any ... I put on the record that when Mr. Traldi refers to the statement of the witness or to his earlier testimony that he should do that as accurately as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to explore some of Mr. Koljevic's views at that time in an attempt to determine whether those are among the views which you had which were identical to his. And we can see him begin speaking at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 9 in the English and 11 in the B/C/S at the bottom, and it's towards the top in the English. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He says: "Instead of denying sovereignty, we tried to offer a surplus of sovereignty. Let it be a sovereign Muslim Bosnia and a sovereign Serbian Bosnia and a sovereign Croatian Bosnia. "Therefore, let it be a sovereign state of sovereign peoples." Now, was dividing Bosnia into sovereign Muslim, Serb, and Croat areas one of the points that you and Mr. Koljevic agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I could have expected anything but a question like this. This was before the war. We agreed to the extent that we needed to fight against war. We agreed that we should try to prevent any crimes from occurring. We agreed that it would be a great shame to breakup Yugoslavia, and so on and so forth. As to what you asked me about now, nobody even could have dreamed then that war would happen and that there would be requests for the sovereignty of this people and that people. Particularly relevant is the fact that I did not attend that meeting. I wasn't even close. Therefore, I really, really must say that I am a bit surprised about getting a question like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- sir, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, there is no need to express your views on the question. Just answer. That's what we expect you to do. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just to repeat my question: Was dividing Bosnia into sovereign Muslim, Serb, and Croat areas one of the points that you and Mr. Koljevic agreed upon; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: That was not discussed so we couldn't have agreed on it. We didn't even speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, he continues --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 12 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "We thought that this could be achieved legally without erecting physical borders, but instead have it organised administratively and politically with complete sovereignty according to the Swiss principle. Now, there is a very interesting thing here. You know that geographically there is a mixture of peoples in Bosnia. That would first require the reconstruction of Bosnian municipalities which have been established to the detriment of the Croatian and Serbian people, and we have established that, that can be established easily." And he goes on and gives the example of Travnik, towards the bottom of the page, which he says is a Croatian town. So was the need to reconstruct the borders of Bosnian municipalities a matter upon which you and Professor Koljevic agreed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: We did not even talk about it, so we couldn't have agreed on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 13 in the English and 17 in the B/C/S. Mr. Boras is discussing specific territories. That's at the top of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he discuss maps, and he says in the middle of the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do we have the right B/C/S version on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's at the very top. And I believe his remarks begin towards the bottom of the previous page. But we could go back to the bottom of page 16 for the clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So that's where he begins speaking and he mentions the maps. And then in the middle of the paragraph says: "We think, however, that this should be preceded by a reorganisation of municipalities, and referendums" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we need the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's actually the only part of his remarks to which I was going to call attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The next speaker, Mr. Manolic responds: "The aim of that reorganisation would be the homogeneity of certain areas." And Mr. Koljevic responds: "Yes, the homogeneity of certain areas." Do you see that in the text before you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I hear it and I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 32 in English and 41 in B/C/S, Mr. Koljevic is speaking again. And he says -- and it's in the middle of the second paragraph in the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "Those enclaves which can be established on the municipal level, they should be delimited and then we should see what can be done with the transfer, what can be accomplished by agreement, and we should institute fair exchanges and create an agency for the civilised transfer of property and population which would be in the interest of those people. The personal 'homogeneity' was, as you know, vilified in Yugoslavia. Why should it be something terrible for people to live with people who are closest to them?" So I'll ask again: Was -- did you and Mr. Koljevic agree that it was desirable to establish ethnically homogenous areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't even remember that we spoke in this way during the war. And before the war this didn't even occur to me. I didn't know anything about it. We did not talk about those problems using those words, Dr. Koljevic and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd tender this document, 65 ter 03202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6727, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6727 is admitted into evidence. Do we need all the 55 pages, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- I think for a fair context of the discussion between what would become two of the warring parties, it's probably best. But I'm happy to discuss the matter with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you would do so and if the parties would agree that a smaller portion would do as well, then that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, you discuss a number of events in Sarajevo in your statement. I have only a few questions about this aspect of your evidence. To start, in paragraph 4, you say you were the representative of the Republika Srpska at UNPROFOR from the 1st of July to the 19th of December 1992. Now, you served as a liaison between the Republika Srpska government and UNPROFOR; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's not. I was just a representative of Republika Srpska with UNPROFOR, and there was a military officer, in the beginning, at least, who was the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now -- and you were the representative of the Bosnian Serb presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I was a representative of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 31229.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And while it comes up, you were appointed to this position by Mr. Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: I was appointed to the position by the president of Republika Srpska, Mr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this isn't translated yet. But if we could look at decision 354, and it's on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if you could just read out the text under point 1 so that it can be interpreted, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: "Decision on the appointment of a temporary representative of the presidency of the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for contact with UNPROFOR. Dr. Vladimir Lukic is appointed temporary representative of the presidency of the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for contacts with UNPROFOR." I do also have a decision to that effect. It's slightly longer but the text to that effect is the same. And I did not read that the decision goes into effect on the day it is reached and it would be published in the Official Gazette of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is the 27th of June 1992 and it's signed by the president of the presidency of the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you reported on your work to President Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: To members of the presidency, depending on who I could reach or whomever got in touch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 15 you state that you received many protest notes from UNPROFOR in relation to incidents which UNPROFOR alleged to be incidents of Bosnian Serb shelling. Many of these protests asserted that the VRS had shelled civilian targets; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: It's correct that I received them, but they were mostly verbal. It was mostly verbal information. They weren't written documents. But I responded with correct information to many of these protests because I could see for myself that what the UNPROFOR drew my attention to wasn't quite correct, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: -- there are plenty of examples where I provided precise data.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in terms of the information you provided in response, you did not have the authority to conduct investigations into such protests yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: Why would I not, as a representative of the government of Republika Srpska, not be able to provide information in instances where my people were getting killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I didn't ask whether you could provide information. I asked whether you had the authority to conduct an investigation yourself. Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, it concerned no investigation. No one gave me any such authority. We never conducted investigations. There was no written correspondence between us and UNPROFOR. We were in the same building, one room next to the other. We regularly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- spoke discussing what was correct or incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I stop you there. You have answered the question that no one had given you any such authority to investigate. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- and -- no, I'm looking at the clock. I'd rather advise you not to proceed at this moment, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Lukic, we'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.30 in the morning. And I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow and perhaps even the day after tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may follow the usher and we'd like to see you back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. You know the rules. Mr. Traldi, there was something you would like to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just so I don't forget tomorrow, Mr. President, if we could have 65 ter 31229 marked for identification pending a translation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the decision of appointment. Is there any dispute --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- about it? Is there any reason to have this as written evidence available?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the date. We have who appointed. It's been read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm in your hands in that regard, Mr. President. I -- I'd used it as a result of the witness's testimony as to who he was the representative of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's accepted. It's marginal whether we really need this kind of evidence, but I'll not -- the Chamber will not obstruct you in tendering it. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P6728, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, marked for identification. We adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, the 9th -- the 10th of -- no, let me. The 9th of September, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of September, 2014, at 9.30 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.21 p.m.,
